items.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998
items.q: And Al Klink played so magnificently. And Tommy Newsom were our chief tenor players.

ctx.x: Clinics. He was suddenly discovering that world. And Rosengarden was always recording someplace, he was always twenty minutes late, and Haggart didn’t want to be there in the first place, and Tony Mottola and Bucky, all of those guys, they rotated the schedule unto themselves, but half the time they’d forget who was there. But it was probably the best, in my opinion, of this period. If you’re going to say — well it was probably the best organization. And it was their organization. Nobody talked. If you talked to…

God forbid, played arpeggios all the time. And we finished this tune and there was silence in 6B, and it was like a Kafka movie where all the — well I think it was thirty seconds, but all this time Mottola took a cloth and cleaned off first his guitar and then put it on the rack and slowly turned around and looked at him. That’s all he did. And we knew it was over, he was gone the next night. But I had many adventures like that. Many. I had Al Klink in that band, who came from the Miller band. He was the, when…
When you listen to — or I don’t know if you do — but when you hear the bands that are playing for the late night shows now—

items.title: Tommy Newsom and Ross Tompkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: He was there with Skitch Henderson and Milton DeLugg.

ctx.x: Oh, he said he just got — Lionel Hampton said if you have any trouble with Benny, just get weirder than he is. And he did that, and I guess it worked for him at the time. Anyway, everybody’s got Benny stories. So you guys were kind of through the years have been alternating between big bands and combos and some studio work.

Yeah, I always play even, well Tommy was with the Tonight Show before I was. He was there with Skitch Henderson and Milton DeLugg. I started when Doc Severinsen started in 1967. But I always went right from there down and played someplace else. If it wasn’t the Half Note it was the Roosevelt Grill or something or the Plaza Nine. There was always some clubs.

Yeah, I asked Ross one day, you know because you spend your whole life working in gin mills and things, you know, low paying jobs, but the jazz scene is usually not high paying generally. And I asked him why he continued to work like down at the Half Note, down in the Village during the Tonight Show. Because you know you work all those years and you’ve got a nice paying job more or less, and he continued to work down there. And I think he explained it this way, he says, “I work at NBC to get cab fare to get down…
